title: How to Build a Cleaning Business Website With AI
metaDescription: A credibility page for a cleaning company: what you cover, what you charge, and one obvious way to get a quote. Built in an afternoon.
body: Cleaning is a trust purchase. Somebody is deciding whether to give a stranger a key to their house, and they are deciding it from a phone in about thirty seconds.

That makes the website's job narrow and specific: look like a real, insured, local business, say exactly what you do and roughly what it costs, and make asking for a quote take one tap. This guide covers building exactly that with Kodely, and what to do about the quote form.
What earns trust on the page

• Where you actually work. Name the towns, postcodes or neighbourhoods. "Serving the local area" reassures nobody and ranks for nothing.
  • What kind of cleaning. Domestic, end of tenancy, commercial, after-builders, oven, carpets. These are different businesses to the person searching.
  • Insurance and checks. Public liability, DBS-checked staff, whatever you genuinely hold. This is usually the single most persuasive line on the page.
  • Prices, or a real price shape. Hourly rate, minimum booking, or a from-price per job. Vagueness reads as expensive.
  • Who you are. A named owner, employed staff or subcontractors, how long you have been going.

All of those are facts about your business, which means you have to supply them. The builder writes a bracketed placeholder like [your insurance details] rather than inventing a policy you do not have — deliberately so.
The quote request: do not use a form
Every cleaning website has a "request a quote" form. Yours should not, and this is the one thing on this page to get right.

A Kodely site is front-end only. There is no server behind it and no mail path, so a form has nowhere to send a submission. It would look entirely convincing and throw away every quote request — including the four-bedroom end-of-tenancy one.
What works instead, with no server at all:

• A large tap-to-call button. For local services this converts better than a form anyway.
  • A mailto: link with the subject line prefilled — "Quote request" — so enquiries arrive pre-sorted.
  • A WhatsApp link, if that is genuinely how your customers talk to you.
  • A link out to a real form tool if you need structured details like room counts.
The full reasoning, and how to wire the button.
Write the prompt

A one-page site for Bright Path Cleaning, a domestic and end-of-tenancy cleaning company covering [your towns]. Run by [your name], [number] employed cleaners, all DBS-checked, [your insurance]. Services with from-prices: regular domestic clean from [price] an hour, one-off deep clean from [price], end of tenancy from [price], oven clean [price]. Minimum booking two hours. Sections: what we do, areas covered as a plain list of place names, why us (insured, checked, employed not subcontracted), prices, and a big "Get a quote" button that is a tap-to-call link, repeated at the top and bottom, plus an email link. No contact form. Clean and calm: white, soft blue-green, one strong accent, generous spacing, plain readable type.
The areas list is doing double duty: it reassures a human and it puts your actual place names in the page text, which is most of what local search needs from a site this size.
If writing that out is more than you want to do, type one line and press Enhance — it expands it into a brief you read and edit before building, and costs no credits.
What it will look like

There will be no photographs — not of your team, not of a sparkling kitchen. Published sites cannot load images from another host and there is no upload path, so the design is carried by type, colour, spacing and inline SVG icons.

For cleaning this is less damaging than you would think. Before-and-after photos are the one thing that would help, and stock photos of someone else's spotless worktop help nobody. What persuades is the insurance line, the postcode list, and a phone number that dials. Why the constraint exists.
Refining and publishing

• "Move the areas covered list higher — it's what people check first."
  • "Make the phone button sticky at the bottom on mobile."
  • "Add 'We bring our own products, including fragrance-free' to the domestic section."
  • "Tone the accent colour down a notch, it's shouting."

Every successful build is a free checkpoint you can roll back to. One click publishes to a kodely.site subdomain with robots.txt and sitemap.xml generated, and a real title and description so a shared link shows your company name.
Start with your areas, your prices and your phone number. See also: the same job for a trade.
